The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 were up in late-morning trading Tuesday, while the Nasdaq Composite was roughly flat, as certain semiconductor stocks sold off.

In company news, Corning (GLW) reported Q2 non-GAAP earnings Tuesday of $0.78 per diluted share, up from $0.60 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus analyst estimate of $0.76. Second-quarter revenue was $4.74 billion, up from $4.05 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $4.63 billion. For Q3, Corning said it expects diluted EPS of $0.85 to $0.89, compared to the FactSet consensus of $0.85. The company said it expects Q3 sales of $4.9 billion to $5 billion, compared to the FactSet consensus of $5 billion. Corning shares were down 15.5% around midday.

Coca-Cola (KO) reported fiscal Q2 comparable diluted EPS Tuesday of $0.97, up from $0.87 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus of $0.93. Net Q2 operating revenue was $13.38 billion, up from $12.54 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $13.17 billion. For 2026, the company said it expects comparable EPS growth of 9% to 10%, up from its previous guidance of 8% to 9%, and it raised its organic growth revenue outlook to about 5% from 4% to 5%. Coca-Cola shares were up 6.0%.

Boeing (BA) reported a Q2 core loss Tuesday of $0.76 per share, narrowing from a loss of $1.24 a year earlier but below the FactSet consensus of a loss of $0.28. Second-quarter revenue was $24.56 billion, up from $2.75 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $24.26 billion. The company said Q2 deliveries increased 14% to 171 planes. Boeing shares were up 4.0%.

Visa (V) confirmed to MT Newswires earlier Tuesday reports that it will trim around 2,600 jobs, or about 7% of it workforce, as part of Chief Executive Ryan McInerney's plan to streamline operations. The cuts will mainly impact its technology and product teams. Visa shares were up 1.2%.

Apple (AAPL) saw its market capitalization surpass $5 trillion for the first time on Tuesday morning, Bloomberg reported. Separately, the company is planning to launch a number of home products, including a hub device built around the new Siri AI assistant, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing people with knowledge of the matter. Apple is also preparing a new TV set-top box and updated HomePod mini, the people reportedly told Bloomberg. Lastly, Apple said Tuesday it has partnered with Klarna Group (KLAR) on a new program that will allow US customers to lease an iPhone for $17.99 per month. In addition to the iPhone, the program, called Apple Upgrade, is offering 12- and 24-month leasing options for Apple Watch, Mac and iPad for $11.99, $24.99 and $11.99 per month, respectively. Apple shares were up 0.8%.

Meta Platforms (META) and BlackRock (BLK) have agreed to form a strategic venture to develop and own a 1-gigawatt data center campus in El Pas, Texas, Meta said Tuesday. Funds managed by BlackRock will own an 80% interest in the joint venture, with Meta holding the remaining 20%, the tech giant said. Meta shares were flat, while BlackRock shares were up 3.2%.

China's Moonshot AI is seeking more Nvidia (NVDA) Blackwell chips, as it discusses plans for Kimi K4, its next model that will be larger than its recently released Kimi K3, The Information reported Tuesday, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia shares were up 0.7%.

Two of Amazon's (AMZN) data centers in Bahrain sustained damage following missile strikes last week that Iran claimed to carry out, Bloomberg reported Tuesday, citing satellite imagery. Amazon shares were down 0.4%.

PayPal (PYPL) reported Q2 non-GAAP EPS Tuesday of $1.38, down from $1.40 a year earlier but above the FactSet consensus of $1.28. Net Q2 revenue was $8.68 billion, up from $8.29 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $8.47 billion. For Q3, the company said it expects to post a roughly low-single-digit decline in non-GAAP EPS from $1.34 a year earlier. Analysts polled by FactSet expect $1.33. For 2026, PayPal expects non-GAAP EPS of about $5.38, above the FactSet consensus of $5.31. Separately, the company said it will offer installment payments for up to 48 months for eligible Amazon customers in Germany and Austria starting in August. PayPal shares were up 3.9%.

Microsoft and Meta Platforms report July 29, and hyperscaler capex commentary will either validate the AI infrastructure trade or accelerate the rotation already underway.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) stock is down 9% in midday Tuesday trading to $453.37, while Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) shares are off 7% to $175.52 and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock is down 6% to $85.82. Meanwhile, Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) shares are also down 7% to $246.37.

MF3d / Getty Images

NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock, by contrast, is up 0.5% to $197.58, and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) shares are down by only 0.5% to $381.30. The split is telling: the AI chip trade is narrowing to its clearest leaders while the higher-beta, richly priced second-tier names are getting trimmed hard.

Flight to the Leaders, Not a Fresh Catalyst

There's no company-specific news driving today's sell-off in AMD, Marvell, Intel, or Arm. Instead, investors appear to be consolidating exposure into the AI infrastructure leaders and cutting back on the crowded, higher-multiple satellites ahead of a heavy Big Tech earnings slate.

The context matters. AMD stock is still up 112% year to date, Marvell shares are up 106%, Intel stock is up 133%, and Arm shares are up 122%. Even after today's drop, these are enormous 2026 gains, and the reaction reads as profit-taking within a big run rather than a fundamental break.

NVIDIA stock, meanwhile, is up only 6% year to date, and Broadcom shares have gained 10%. The leaders haven't stretched as far, which is exactly why capital is rotating toward them today.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and AMD didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today.

Valuation Jitters Are Doing the Work

The dispersion in trailing multiples helps explain the price action. NVIDIA trades at a trailing P/E ratio of 30.28x, and Broadcom sits at 63.14x. Marvell is at 60.27x, AMD carries a 150.54x multiple, and Arm stock trades at a striking 289.41x. Intel isn't profitable on a trailing 12-month basis, so there's no meaningful TTM P/E ratio to anchor its valuation.

The pattern lines up neatly with today's action. The names holding up carry more moderate multiples, and the hardest-hit names are either the most richly valued (Arm, AMD) or unprofitable (Intel). That's the definition of a valuation reset inside a crowded theme.

title: 4 US Stocks Earnings to Watch This Week: Will AI Spending Finally Pay Off?
detail:
4 US Stocks Earnings to Watch This Week: Will AI Spending Finally Pay Off?

Trading disclosure

Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon are the four US stocks with earnings to watch this week. Investors care less about profit beats than about whether record AI spending is producing revenue.

Alphabet already set the bar on July 22. Its shares fell despite beating on nearly every line, punished for lifting full-year capital spending guidance toward $205 billion.

Why Alphabet's Selloff Reset Big Tech Earnings Expectations

Alphabet posted second-quarter revenue of $119.8 billion, a 24% annual increase. Diluted earnings reached $9.11 a share. Google Cloud revenue climbed 82% to $24.8 billion.

The stock still dropped roughly 4% after hours. Management had raised 2026 capital expenditure guidance to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion. The prior range topped out at $190 billion.

Google Stock Performance. Source: Yahoo Finance

Quarterly capital spending hit $44.9 billion, roughly double the year-earlier figure. Free cash flow turned negative at $5.9 billion.

That combination is the new market test. Beating on revenue no longer protects a stock if spending guidance rises faster.

What the Latest Filings Already Reveal About AI Capex

Most coverage treats AI spending as a forecast. The filings show it has already landed.

BeInCrypto reviewed the most recent quarterly cash flow statements for all five companies. The pattern is consistent. Capital spending is growing far faster than the cash generated to fund it.

Microsoft offers the clearest example. Additions to property and equipment reached $30.9 billion in the March quarter, according to its filing. That is up 84% from $16.7 billion a year earlier.

Operating cash flow grew far more slowly. Subtract capital spending and the remainder fell 22% to $15.8 billion, even though net income rose 23%.

Depreciation tells the same story. Microsoft's depreciation and amortization charge rose 31% to $10.2 billion. Meta's climbed 54% to $6.0 billion.

This is a pattern rather than a single quarter. Microsoft spent $80.1 billion on property and equipment across the first nine months of its fiscal year, up 69% from $47.5 billion.

Figures calculated by BeInCrypto from company cash flow statements. Amazon reports free cash flow on a trailing twelve-month basis.

Amazon shows the sharpest deterioration. Trailing free cash flow fell to $1.2 billion from $25.9 billion a year earlier. The company attributed the drop to a $59.3 billion rise in equipment purchases.

Combined Big Tech AI capex guidance for 2026 now runs into the hundreds of billions. The reported figures show that spending arriving on the balance sheet ahead of the revenue meant to justify it.

The revenue side is not standing still, however. Azure grew 40% last quarter, Google Cloud 82%, and Amazon Web Services 28%. The open question concerns timing rather than demand.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) returned 45% year to date while its most famous constituent barely participated. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) is up only 11.04% YTD, weighed down by the China H20 overhang and a valuation reset even as the business itself printed 85.23% revenue growth in Q1 FY27.

Canva | AndreyPopov from Getty Images and 400tmax from Getty Images Signature

SMH thrived despite NVIDIA lagging, which is a different and more interesting story about what the fund does.

The rally that stopped being one stock

For two years, owning SMH was mostly a leveraged bet on Jensen Huang's roadmap. In 2026, the engine changed. Memory ripped first. Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is up 158% YTD on severe DRAM and HBM shortages, with fiscal Q3 revenue up 345.7% year over year and HBM4 already in high-volume shipments. Then the inference and agentic-AI wave lifted the CPU/GPU also-rans: Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) climbed 102% on the Meta 6-gigawatt MI450 win, and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) somehow rallied 115% as CEO Lip-Bu Tan delivered the strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years.

Equipment makers rode the capex tide. ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML) is up 35% YTD after raising its FY26 guide and telling investors it will add 30% more low-NA EUV capacity for 2027. When NVIDIA underperforms, and your fund still compounds at over 56%, something structural is happening beneath the ticker.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now.

Obviously, most of these semiconductor names are selling off sharply as of this writing, but they're still sitting atop historic year-to-date gains.

How the index rulebook did the work

SMH tracks the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor 25 Index, which imposes a per-position weight cap and rebalances quarterly. Sources on the exact cap conflict, so treat it qualitatively: when any single holding, NVIDIA included, blows through the ceiling between rebalances, the next reset trims it.

That is why, per the May 27, 2026 fact sheet, AMD sits at the top at 10.33%, ahead of Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) at 9.57%, Micron at 9.39%, TSMC (NYSE:TSM) at 8.75%, and NVIDIA at only 8.40%. A discretionary manager would have been tempted to let NVIDIA compound to 25% of the book. The rulebook did not permit it. That mechanic, boring on the way up, protected the fund on the way down.

I keep buying Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), and last weeks earnings gave me another reason to add. For three years I have been asking one question about this position: is the AI spend actually turning into revenue that scales? Q2 answered it plainly.

24/7 Wall St.

Google Cloud grew 82% year over year to $24.77 billion. That is a fourth straight quarter of accelerating growth off a base already at scale: 34%, then 48%, then 63%, now 82%. Sundar Pichai told shareholders "nearly 90% of the Fortune 100" is now using Gemini Enterprise. That is a competitive moat forming in real time, and it is why I keep coming back to the buy button.

The Numbers Behind My Conviction

Revenue landed at $119.80 billion, up 24.23% YoY, the 12th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth. EPS printed at $9.11 against a $3.0427 estimate, the 11th consecutive beat. Operating income rose 30.38% to $40.77 billion, with operating margin expanding 2 percentage points to 34%. Alphabet is growing at the top and widening the funnel at the same time.

The AI adoption data is what convinces me the growth is durable. Gemini API traffic reached 22 billion tokens per minute, up from 7 billion three quarters ago. The Gemini App now has 950 million monthly active users, versus 650 million in Q3 FY25. Search itself grew 17% because AI features are lifting query volume, not cannibalizing it. That is the payoff I was waiting on.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Google didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today.

The balance sheet supports the aggression: cash and equivalents at $55.91 billion, shareholders' equity at $640.48 billion, and the dividend was raised 5% to $0.22 per share. Yield is thin at 0.50%, but the direction of travel is what a long-term holder wants.

Why Not Microsoft, Meta, or Amazon?

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) are the names a retirement-focused reader reaches for first, and I own pieces of them. What tips my next dollar toward Alphabet is the Cloud acceleration curve: 34% to 48% to 63% to 82% across four quarters, off a segment that just cleared $24.77 billion in a single quarter and a Q1 backlog above $460 billion. Paying 27x earnings for that runway, at a $4.24 trillion business, is a trade I keep making.
